title: The Daily Prayer Rhythm in Mecca
description: Faith label: tradition. In Islamic tradition and practice, Muslims pray five times each day, at dawn, midday, afternoon, sunset, and night, and in Mecca that rhythm is set by the Grand Mosque, whose calls to prayer organise the day for residents and visitors alike. Shops pause, streets fill and empty, and the mosque precinct fills for each prayer, so the day in Mecca has a visible, audible pulse that follows the prayer times. This record describes that rhythm in general terms; it does not give a timetable, and its daylight demo is an approximate educational model, never a prayer timetable and never religious authority. Prayer in the Grand Mosque is congregational: worshippers stand in rows facing the Kaaba, following one leader, and the scale of the congregation is part of the experience described by visitors, with rows extending across the mosque's courtyards and plazas. Visitors are expected to follow the mosque's general guidance on dress, conduct, and movement, and to join or step aside respectfully according to the mosque's own arrangements. No individual instruction is given here, because practice details vary and mosque guidance is the proper source for them. The factual layer is simple and is labeled fact: prayer times move through the year with the sun, so the daily rhythm shifts seasonally, and the mosque precinct's capacity and facilities are matters of published building data, not of tradition. Tradition and fact meet in the rhythm itself: a tradition of five daily prayers, kept in a real city, on real days, with real crowds.

TITLE = 'Daily Prayer Rhythm Daylight Model'
import math
DAY = 100; LAT = 21.3891
decl = -23.44 * math.cos(math.radians(360.0 / 365.0 * (DAY + 10)))
lat = math.radians(LAT); dec = math.radians(decl)
cos_h = -math.tan(lat) * math.tan(dec)
cos_h = max(-1.0, min(1.0, cos_h))
daylen = 2 * math.degrees(math.acos(cos_h)) / 15.0
sunrise = 12 - daylen / 2; sunset = 12 + daylen / 2
print("APPROXIMATE daylight model: " + TITLE)
print("Day of year (fixed input, not today): %d" % DAY)
print("Solar declination: %.1f degrees" % decl)
print("Approximate daylight: %.2f hours" % daylen)
print("Approximate sunrise (solar time): %.2f" % sunrise)
print("Approximate sunset (solar time): %.2f" % sunset)
print("NOTE: approximate educational model only; never religious authority and never a prayer timetable.")

In Mecca, visitors and residents practise supplication and remembrance in the mosque precinct, on the walkways, and in quiet corners, in words they choose themselves or in traditional phrases they have learned, and the practice is personal: its words, its length, and its occasion vary with the person. This record paraphrases only and invents no wording, because inventing devotional wording would be inventing doctrine, which this database never does. Traditions differ in emphasis: some communities stress particular times or gatherings for remembrance, others stress private, individual practice, and this record states that difference rather than settling it. What the traditions share, in general terms, is the idea that remembrance is not confined to the mosque or to set times, but belongs to ordinary life as well, and Mecca's precinct, with its constant flow of people, is a place where that idea is visibly lived. No ruling is given here about what any individual should say or when, and no quotation is offered. Readers who want traditional wordings should consult published collections and qualified teachers, and this record's contribution is a general description of the practice and its place in Meccan devotional life.

title: Sacred Nights: Tradition, Meaning, and Differences
description: Faith label: tradition, with differences stated. In Islamic tradition, certain nights are held in special regard, above all the nights of Ramadan and, within Ramadan, the last ten nights, among which tradition places a night of great value whose exact date is, in tradition itself, not fixed to a single night. That uncertainty is part of the tradition: because the night is not pinned to one date, tradition encourages devotion across the last ten nights rather than on one night alone. This record reports that as tradition, and it does not fix a date. Traditions differ on other nights as well: communities differ in how they mark the middle night of the month of Shaban, the night of the ascension, and other nights held significant in various traditions, and some communities mark a night that others do not mark at all. This record states that traditions differ and does not settle those differences, because settling them would be issuing a ruling, which this database never does. A general description of a night's observance in one community must never be read as a rule for all communities. In Mecca, sacred nights are marked by extended night prayers, recitation, and supplication in the Grand Mosque, in general terms, and the precinct's night-time crowds on those nights are a factual matter of crowd observation. Tradition layer: the nights' significance is tradition. Fact layer: the gatherings themselves are observable. No quotation, no date-fixing, and no ruling appears here.

title: Teaching Circles in the Grand Mosque
description: Faith label: fact for the circles' existence and general form, tradition for their subject matter. Teaching circles, known in Arabic as halaqat, are a long-standing general feature of the Grand Mosque: a teacher sits with students in a circle, often after a prayer, and teaches recitation, law, language, or tradition, with students of all ages and backgrounds joining and leaving as they wish. The circles are open in form, public in setting, and varied in subject, and they are one of the mosque's oldest educational institutions, predating modern classrooms. The form is factual and observable: circles gather in the mosque's courtyards and halls, teachers are appointed or recognised by the mosque authorities, and sessions follow the prayer rhythm of the day. The content is tradition: what is taught is Islamic tradition, and this record does not summarise any circle's teaching, because teaching content varies by teacher and by session and is properly learned in the circle itself, not from a database summary. Women and men have their own circles and arrangements, following the mosque's own organisation, which this record notes in general terms only. Modern teaching adds broadcasts, recordings, and published lessons to the circle form, so a student can now follow a circle from far away, but the circle itself remains a face-to-face gathering. That continuity, an old form carried into new media, is the general point of this record, and it is stated without endorsing any individual teacher or circle.

title: Spiritual Etiquette for Visitors to Mecca
description: Faith label: fact. This record gives general, respectful guidance for visitors to Mecca's sacred precinct, drawn from published visitor guidance, and it is not a ruling for any individual. Dress modestly, in line with the mosque's published guidance; remove shoes where the mosque requires it; keep voices low in prayer areas; do not photograph people without consideration for their worship; and follow the directions of mosque staff and crowd marshals, especially at gates and during peak prayer times. Those points are general conduct guidance, not religious rulings, and mosque staff guidance on the day takes precedence over any general description here. Entry restriction, stated factually and without any workaround: entry to Mecca's central sacred area is restricted to Muslims under Saudi regulation, with checkpoints and signage on the roads into the city. This record gives no evasion, circumvention, or workaround of that restriction in any form, and it does not suggest any method of entering the restricted area without meeting the regulation. Visitors who are not Muslim are welcome to learn about Mecca through published books, exhibitions, broadcasts, and this database, and visitors who are Muslim should check current official Saudi guidance before travel, because requirements and arrangements change. Health and safety guidance is also factual: heat, crowds, and long walks demand water, rest, sun protection, and attention to official health requirements, and pilgrims with medical conditions should seek medical advice before travel. This record gives no medical advice for any individual and no travel advice for any individual; it points the reader to current official sources for both.

title: Mecca in Poetry and Literature
description: Faith label: fact. Mecca appears across centuries of Arabic and world literature, in poetry, travel writing, and pilgrimage accounts, and those works are published, datable facts that a reader can check. Classical Arabic poets wrote of Mecca and the pilgrimage in verses that are still anthologised and studied, medieval and early modern travellers wrote pilgrimage accounts describing the city, its mosque, and its markets in the terms of their own centuries, and modern writers, novelists, and memoirists continue to write about Mecca, pilgrimage, and return. This record names no passage and quotes none, because quotation would require verified text, and its purpose is a general map of the literature, not an anthology. Pilgrimage accounts are also historical sources in their own right: a traveller's description of Mecca's gates, markets, water, and crowds in a given century is evidence for that century's city, even when the traveller's impressions are coloured by their own background. Reading several accounts together, across centuries, shows the city changing: walls and gates giving way to modern streets, small crowds becoming millions, and the mosque precinct growing around its centre. That comparative reading is the literary record's value to this pair. Modern literature about Mecca includes novels, memoirs, and reportage in many languages, and the field continues to grow as new pilgrims write. This record does not rank works or endorse any author, and it notes that works about a sacred city by non-Muslim authors exist alongside works by Muslim authors, with different standpoints that a careful reader should notice. A full bibliography is not in the public record as a single list, and this record does not invent one.

Taraweeh (tradition): extended congregational night prayers in Ramadan, in which portions of the Quran are recited. Halaqa (fact for the form, tradition for the content): a teaching circle in the mosque, a teacher with students gathered around. Qibla (fact for the direction, tradition for its meaning): the direction of prayer toward the Kaaba, measurable from any location. Supplication (tradition): personal prayer calling upon God, in words chosen by the worshipper or learned from tradition, paraphrased here only. Remembrance (tradition): the repeated mention of God's names and praises, as a devotional practice. Ramadan (tradition): the month of fasting in Islamic tradition. Sacred nights (tradition, differences stated): nights held in special regard in tradition, with communities differing on which nights and how they are marked. Each entry states its layer: fact where the term names a measurable or observable thing, tradition where it names a devotional meaning. Where a term carries both layers, both are stated, and neither is allowed to stand in for the other.
